sites.name: Desierto de Atacama
sites.elevation_text: Aproximadamente entre 2,000 y 4,500 m; edificios volcánicos sobre 5,500 m
sites.coordinate_note: Las coordenadas representan aproximadamente la región y no un punto específico de muestreo.
sites.terrain_classification: Aridez extrema; Superficies rocosas y pedregosas; Cuencas sedimentarias; Depósitos salinos y evaporíticos; Terrenos volcánicos; Procesos eólicos; Microorganismos adaptados a ambientes extremos.
sites.description:
El Desierto de Atacama es una región del norte de Chile caracterizada por condiciones de aridez extrema y una notable diversidad geológica. Contiene planicies desérticas, terrenos volcánicos, cuencas salinas, depósitos sedimentarios y superficies rocosas.

Estas características permiten estudiar determinados procesos geológicos y ambientales relacionados con la exploración planetaria, así como desarrollar pruebas de movilidad robótica, reconocimiento del terreno e instrumentos científicos.

assessments.objective:
Analizar las características topográficas, térmicas, geológicas, ambientales y subterráneas del Desierto de Atacama para determinar su utilidad como entorno terrestre de pruebas relacionadas con la exploración lunar.

La evaluación considera tanto las semejanzas entre los terrenos como sus diferencias físicas y ambientales.
assessments.characterization:
El Desierto de Atacama se encuentra en el norte de Chile y comprende terrenos hiperáridos, cuencas sedimentarias, superficies pedregosas, depósitos salinos, laderas montañosas y sectores volcánicos.

En las pampas interiores existen amplias superficies secas y relativamente planas, mientras que las áreas cordilleranas presentan pendientes abruptas y terrenos más accidentados.

Su diversidad geológica permite desarrollar ensayos de reconocimiento del terreno, movilidad robótica y exploración de estructuras naturales.
assessments.conclusion:
El Desierto de Atacama obtiene una similitud exploratoria general de 31.2 %, correspondiente a una clasificación baja.

Sus principales oportunidades se encuentran en pruebas operativas relacionadas con topografía, movilidad y reconocimiento de estructuras naturales.

Atacama puede considerarse un análogo lunar parcial para aplicaciones específicas, especialmente cuando se combina con ensayos especializados que reproduzcan las condiciones físicas no presentes en la Tierra.
assessments.limitations:
Atacama no reproduce la gravedad lunar, el vacío, la radiación espacial, los ciclos térmicos lunares ni las propiedades completas del regolito lunar.

Por tanto, su utilidad depende de la tecnología o el proceso que se desee estudiar.
assessments.methodology:
La evaluación compara características descriptivas del entorno terrestre con variables planetarias de referencia. Los porcentajes corresponden al sistema exploratorio de puntuación utilizado en el prototipo. No son mediciones directas de las misiones citadas ni resultados de una fórmula cuantitativa validada. La escala empleada es:

● Muy alta: 90–100 %. ● Alta: 75–menos de 90 %. ● Moderada: 50–menos de 75 %. ● Baja: 25–menos de 50 %. ● Muy baja: 0–menos de 25 %. ● No aplicable: N/A. Las puntuaciones no aplicables se excluyen de los cálculos. Para validar los resultados en una fase posterior será necesario delimitar sitios específicos, utilizar mediciones comparables y documentar una fórmula reproducible.

variables.label: Elevación
variables.explanation: Los terrenos de Atacama alcanzan aproximadamente entre 2,000 y 4,500 metros en los sectores considerados. La Luna presenta elevaciones y depresiones medidas respecto de un sistema de referencia diferente. La analogía se relaciona principalmente con la presencia de terrenos elevados y desniveles, no con la equivalencia directa de altitudes.
variables.utility: estudiar operaciones robóticas en terrenos de distinta altitud.

variables.label: Pendiente
variables.explanation: Las planicies aluviales y salares pueden presentar pendientes suaves, mientras que algunas laderas montañosas superan los 30°. Esta variedad permite representar determinados desafíos de desplazamiento sobre superficies inclinadas.
variables.utility: probar ascenso, descenso, estabilidad y tracción de rovers.

variables.label: Rugosidad
variables.explanation: Las costras salinas fracturadas, superficies pedregosas y acumulaciones de fragmentos producen irregularidades que pueden dificultar el movimiento de vehículos.
variables.utility: evaluar suspensión, ruedas, tracción y detección de irregularidades.

variables.label: Relieve
variables.explanation: Atacama contiene pampas, abanicos aluviales, cuencas y cordones montañosos. Estas formas no reproducen directamente la diversidad del relieve lunar, donde destacan cráteres de impacto y otras estructuras.
variables.utility: desarrollar reconocimiento del terreno y planificación de rutas.

variables.label: Cráteres
variables.explanation: Los cráteres de impacto no constituyen una característica dominante de Atacama. Algunas depresiones salinas o estructuras volcánicas pueden parecerse visualmente a cráteres, pero tienen orígenes distintos.
variables.utility: identificar las limitaciones de las simulaciones de terrenos lunares.

variables.label: Obstáculos superficiales
variables.explanation: Los bloques rocosos, grietas y costras fracturadas representan obstáculos relevantes para vehículos de exploración.
variables.utility: probar detección de obstáculos, evasión y navegación autónoma.

categories.utility: Ensayos de movilidad robótica, navegación autónoma y reconocimiento geomorfológico.

variables.label: Temperatura superficial
variables.explanation: En sectores expuestos del desierto, las superficies pueden calentarse intensamente durante el día y enfriarse por la noche. La Luna presenta un régimen térmico mucho más extremo debido a la ausencia de una atmósfera significativa y a sus largos ciclos de iluminación.
variables.utility: evaluar parcialmente sensores térmicos.

variables.label: Temperaturas máximas y mínimas
variables.explanation: La investigación terrestre identifica máximas superficiales elevadas y mínimas bajo cero en determinados sectores. Los extremos lunares son mucho más amplios.
variables.utility: determinar qué condiciones requieren simuladores térmicos especializados.

variables.label: Variación térmica
variables.explanation: La aridez y la baja nubosidad favorecen cambios importantes entre el día y la noche en Atacama. Sin embargo, los ciclos lunares tienen una duración y amplitud distintas.
variables.utility: realizar ensayos preliminares de resistencia a variaciones de temperatura.

variables.label: Iluminación solar
variables.explanation: Los cielos despejados de Atacama favorecen una elevada exposición solar. La distribución de luz y sombra en la Luna depende de su relieve y de su ciclo de iluminación.
variables.utility: probar cámaras, sensores ópticos y sistemas de captación solar.

variables.label: Presión atmosférica y vacío
variables.explanation: Atacama posee una atmósfera terrestre, mientras que la Luna presenta condiciones próximas al vacío.
variables.utility: identificar la necesidad de cámaras de vacío para ensayos ambientales lunares.

categories.utility: Pruebas ambientales parciales de equipos, sensores y sistemas ópticos.

variables.label: Tipo de roca
variables.explanation: En Atacama se encuentran ignimbritas, andesitas, basaltos y materiales sedimentarios evaporíticos. La Luna presenta principalmente materiales ígneos y depósitos modificados por impactos.
variables.utility: ensayar identificación y clasificación de rocas.

variables.label: Composición mineralógica
variables.explanation: Atacama contiene silicatos, cuarzo, plagioclasas, arcillas y minerales salinos. Existen algunas familias minerales relacionadas con las lunares, pero las asociaciones y abundancias son diferentes.
variables.utility: probar instrumentos de reconocimiento mineralógico.

variables.label: Composición química
variables.explanation: Los materiales terrestres presentan compuestos asociados con agua, oxidación y procesos atmosféricos. La química de los materiales lunares refleja una historia geológica distinta.
variables.utility: realizar ensayos preliminares de análisis geoquímico.

variables.label: Material superficial
variables.explanation: Las arenas, pavimentos desérticos y fragmentos rocosos permiten estudiar el comportamiento de equipos sobre terrenos granulares. No reproducen completamente el regolito lunar.
variables.utility: probar movilidad, excavación y contacto mecánico con el terreno.

variables.label: Alteración geológica
variables.explanation: Atacama presenta meteorización física, química y eólica. En la Luna predominan procesos asociados con impactos e intemperismo espacial.
variables.utility: comparar procesos de modificación superficial y sus efectos sobre los materiales.

variables.label: Formaciones geológicas
variables.explanation: Los edificios volcánicos, coladas y estructuras rocosas de Atacama permiten realizar determinados estudios comparativos con terrenos volcánicos lunares.
variables.utility: ensayar reconocimiento de estructuras volcánicas.

categories.utility: Reconocimiento de rocas, análisis de materiales y pruebas de instrumentos.

variables.label: Agua superficial
variables.explanation: El núcleo hiperárido de Atacama presenta muy poca agua superficial, aunque existen salares, acuíferos y otros ambientes con agua en la región.
variables.utility: estudiar operaciones en terrenos secos.

variables.label: Hielo superficial
variables.explanation: El hielo de alta montaña terrestre se encuentra bajo condiciones atmosféricas y térmicas diferentes de las de los depósitos lunares.
variables.utility: ensayar técnicas de reconocimiento de hielo.

variables.label: Hielo subterráneo
variables.explanation: La investigación disponible no establece una correspondencia directa entre los materiales subterráneos de Atacama y los posibles depósitos lunares.
variables.utility: evaluar métodos de detección subsuperficial.

variables.label: Permafrost
variables.explanation: En sectores andinos de gran altitud pueden existir terrenos permanentemente congelados. Su comportamiento difiere de las condiciones criogénicas lunares.
variables.utility: realizar pruebas parciales en suelos fríos.

variables.label: Hidrógeno
variables.explanation: Algunos minerales terrestres contienen hidrógeno asociado con agua o grupos hidroxilo. Esto no implica equivalencia con las señales de hidrógeno detectadas en la Luna.
variables.utility: desarrollar conceptos de reconocimiento de materiales hidratados.

variables.label: Recursos minerales
variables.explanation: Atacama presenta depósitos de litio, nitratos, boratos y otras sales. Los recursos lunares prioritarios y sus métodos de aprovechamiento son diferentes.
variables.utility: ensayar clasificación mineral y procedimientos de prospección.

categories.utility: Pruebas preliminares de reconocimiento de recursos y análisis de materiales.

variables.label: Viento
variables.explanation: El viento transporta partículas en Atacama. La Luna no presenta circulación atmosférica equivalente.
variables.utility: distinguir los procesos de transporte superficial.

variables.label: Polvo abrasivo
variables.explanation: Los materiales finos y fragmentados de Atacama pueden provocar desgaste mecánico en equipos. El polvo lunar presenta propiedades físicas diferentes.
variables.utility: probar medidas preliminares de protección contra partículas.

variables.label: Erosión eólica
variables.explanation: La erosión por viento modifica las superficies terrestres, pero no constituye un proceso equivalente en la Luna.
variables.utility: identificar diferencias geomorfológicas.

variables.label: Sedimentos y dunas
variables.explanation: Los depósitos granulares de Atacama pueden utilizarse para ensayos mecánicos, aunque su transporte y acumulación ocurren mediante procesos distintos de los lunares.
variables.utility: estudiar movilidad y comportamiento de materiales granulares.

categories.utility: Evaluación de interacción entre equipos y partículas.

variables.label: Cuevas y tubos de lava
variables.explanation: La investigación terrestre identifica cavidades salinas y posibles estructuras volcánicas en determinados sectores. Las cavidades lunares presentan condiciones ambientales y geológicas distintas.
variables.utility: probar robots, sensores y navegación en espacios confinados.

variables.label: Fracturas tectónicas
variables.explanation: Las fallas y fracturas de Atacama ofrecen oportunidades para ensayar reconocimiento de discontinuidades del terreno.
variables.utility: desarrollar técnicas de cartografía estructural.

variables.label: Estructura estratigráfica
variables.explanation: Las secuencias terrestres contienen depósitos sedimentarios y volcánicos. Los estratos lunares responden a procesos diferentes.
variables.utility: probar técnicas de análisis de capas geológicas.

variables.label: Espesor de regolito
variables.explanation: Los espesores y propiedades de los materiales superficiales terrestres difieren de los del regolito lunar.
variables.utility: evaluar procedimientos de sondeo y exploración superficial.

categories.utility: Exploración robótica de cavidades y reconocimiento de estructuras.

variables.label: Similitud biológica directa
variables.explanation: La existencia de microorganismos en Atacama no implica una correspondencia con organismos lunares.
variables.utility: delimitar las aplicaciones biológicas y estudiar requisitos ambientales de futuras operaciones.

assessments.objective:
Analizar las semejanzas geológicas, geomorfológicas, térmicas, ambientales y astrobiológicas entre el Desierto de Atacama y determinados ambientes de Marte.

La evaluación busca identificar aplicaciones científicas y tecnológicas para la exploración planetaria, especialmente reconocimiento geológico, movilidad robótica, análisis de materiales y estudios de habitabilidad.
assessments.characterization:
Atacama presenta condiciones de aridez extrema, terrenos volcánicos, depósitos sedimentarios, superficies rocosas, cuencas salinas y comunidades microbianas adaptadas a ambientes difíciles.

Estas características permiten estudiar determinados procesos relacionados con la historia geológica y ambiental de Marte.

La región es heterogénea: las condiciones de las pampas hiperáridas, salares y zonas volcánicas no son idénticas.
assessments.conclusion:
El Desierto de Atacama obtiene una similitud exploratoria general de 68.4 %, correspondiente a una clasificación moderada.

La categoría de mayor similitud es geología y mineralogía, con 78.4 %, seguida por biología y habitabilidad, con 72.5 %, y atmósfera, polvo y dinámica eólica, con 71.3 %.

Atacama constituye un entorno de interés para investigaciones relacionadas con Marte, especialmente en geoquímica, mineralogía, astrobiología y pruebas de tecnologías de exploración.

Su utilidad científica es mayor cuando se seleccionan sectores específicos del desierto de acuerdo con los objetivos de investigación.
assessments.limitations:
Atacama no reproduce completamente:

● La gravedad marciana. ● La baja presión atmosférica. ● La composición atmosférica de Marte. ● Las condiciones térmicas marcianas. ● La radiación espacial. ● La distribución regional del hielo y otros recursos.

Las semejanzas deben interpretarse en relación con procesos o aplicaciones concretas.
assessments.methodology:
La evaluación considera siete categorías de comparación y sus subvariables.

Los porcentajes proceden del sistema exploratorio de puntuación utilizado en el prototipo. No son mediciones directas de las misiones citadas ni resultados de una fórmula cuantitativa validada.

La clasificación utilizada es:

● Muy alta: 90–100 %. ● Alta: 75–menos de 90 %. ● Moderada: 50–menos de 75 %. ● Baja: 25–menos de 50 %. ● Muy baja: 0–menos de 25 %.

La validación posterior requerirá delimitar regiones de referencia, obtener mediciones comparables y documentar una fórmula de cálculo reproducible.

assessments.objective: This assessment examines the suitability of the Mauna Kea–Kīlauea volcanic environments for terrestrial tests relevant to lunar exploration. It emphasizes basaltic geology, surface mobility, volcanic landforms, and subsurface structures.
assessments.characterization:
The Hawaiian volcanic complex contains basaltic shield volcanoes, lava fields, cinder deposits, volcanic craters, fractures, and lava tubes. Mauna Kea reaches approximately 4,207 m above sea level and experiences cold summit conditions. Kīlauea includes active volcanic processes and relatively young basaltic surfaces.

The complex is not environmentally uniform. Humid lowland terrain, high-altitude volcanic slopes, and relatively dry lava fields must be evaluated separately when designing experiments.
assessments.conclusion:
The Hawaii Volcanic Complex receives a provisional lunar similarity score of 55.0%, classified as Moderate.

Its strongest assessed categories are Subsurface and Natural Structures (91.0%), Geology and Mineralogy (87.0%), and Topography and Geomorphology (76.0%).

The most valuable application is the investigation of basaltic volcanic terrain and underground structures potentially relevant to lunar exploration.
assessments.limitations:
The Hawaiian environment does not reproduce lunar gravity, near-vacuum conditions, prolonged lunar thermal cycles, space radiation, micrometeorite exposure, or the complete properties of lunar regolith.

Its usefulness is therefore greatest for targeted geological and operational tests rather than full environmental simulation.
assessments.methodology:
The assessment uses the supplied terrestrial and lunar research to identify geological, environmental, and operational similarities. The displayed scores are provisional qualitative judgments for the prototype, not direct measurements from the referenced missions or the output of a validated quantitative similarity model.

The classification scale is Very high (90–100%), High (75–less than 90%), Moderate (50–less than 75%), Low (25–less than 50%), Very low (0–less than 25%), and Not applicable (N/A).

A reproducible scientific score would require defined geographic sampling areas, comparable physical measurements, explicit variable weights, and documented normalization procedures.

assessments.objective: This assessment evaluates the suitability of Mauna Kea and Kīlauea as terrestrial analog environments for Martian volcanic terrain, geological exploration, subsurface reconnaissance, and selected astrobiological investigations.
assessments.characterization:
The Hawaiian volcanic complex is dominated by basaltic shield volcanism. Its landscapes include lava flows, volcanic craters, cinder deposits, fractures, and lava tubes.

Mauna Kea provides high-altitude volcanic terrain and cold summit conditions. Kīlauea provides active volcanic processes and relatively young basaltic surfaces.

These features offer useful comparisons with Martian volcanic regions, including the large shield volcanoes of Tharsis and other basaltic terrains.

However, Hawaiian atmospheric conditions, biological activity, and water availability differ substantially from present-day Mars.
assessments.conclusion:
The Hawaii Volcanic Complex receives a provisional Martian similarity score of 63.3%, classified as Moderate.

The highest assessed categories are Subsurface and Natural Structures (87.0%), Geology and Mineralogy (85.0%), and Topography and Geomorphology (82.0%).

Hawaii is especially valuable for testing geological and robotic exploration methods in basaltic volcanic environments. Its suitability for atmospheric, cryogenic, and comprehensive environmental simulations is more limited.
assessments.limitations:
Hawaii does not reproduce Martian gravity, atmospheric composition, low atmospheric pressure, widespread cold conditions, space radiation, or the distribution of Martian subsurface ice.

Its humid and biologically active environments also differ from much of the present Martian surface.
assessments.methodology:
This evaluation compares the terrestrial characteristics described in the supplied Hawaiian research with global and regional Martian observations.

The prototype percentages represent provisional qualitative similarity judgments. They are not direct NASA measurements or the result of a validated numerical scoring algorithm.

assessments.objective:
This assessment examines Iceland’s suitability as a terrestrial analog for selected lunar geological environments and exploration operations.

It focuses on basaltic volcanic terrain, surface roughness, natural underground structures, frozen-ground environments, and the practical testing of robotic exploration technologies.
assessments.characterization:
Iceland is a volcanic island along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Its terrain includes extensive basaltic lava fields, volcanic fissures, calderas, glacial valleys, black volcanic sands, and lava-tube systems.

Its highest point, Hvannadalshnúkur, reaches approximately 2,110 m above sea level. The island also contains major ice caps, including Vatnajökull, Langjökull, and Hofsjökull.

The landscape is shaped by active volcanism, tectonic extension, glacial erosion, hydrothermal alteration, and atmospheric processes.

These conditions make Iceland valuable for specific geological and operational studies, but they also distinguish it from the dry, nearly airless lunar surface.
assessments.conclusion:
Iceland receives a provisional lunar similarity score of 54.5%, classified as Moderate.

Its strongest assessed categories are Subsurface and Natural Structures (87.0%), Geology and Mineralogy (74.0%), and Topography and Geomorphology (66.0%).

The most valuable lunar analog applications involve lava-tube exploration, basaltic terrain navigation, and geological instrument testing.
assessments.limitations:
Iceland does not reproduce lunar gravity, near-vacuum conditions, extreme lunar thermal cycles, space radiation, or the complete mechanical and chemical properties of lunar regolith.

Its glacial erosion, active hydrological systems, and hydrothermal alteration also differ from the dominant geological processes of the present lunar surface.

The site is therefore most useful for targeted volcanic, robotic, and subsurface experiments rather than complete lunar environmental simulation.

assessments.objective:
This assessment evaluates Iceland as a terrestrial analog for selected Martian volcanic, glacial, periglacial, sedimentary, and potentially habitable environments.

The analysis emphasizes basaltic geology, cold-region processes, ice-bearing terrain, wind-driven sediment transport, subsurface structures, and the investigation of microbial survival in extreme terrestrial environments.
assessments.characterization:
Iceland is a geologically active volcanic island influenced by the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and interactions between volcanism, glaciers, groundwater, and atmospheric processes.

Its landscapes include basaltic lava fields, volcanic fissures, calderas, glacial valleys, black-sand deserts, geothermal systems, lava tubes, and localized mountain permafrost.

Major glaciers, including Vatnajökull, Langjökull, and Hofsjökull, provide extensive ice-bearing environments. Iceland also contains subglacial volcanic deposits, palagonitic rocks, hydrothermally altered minerals, and microbial communities adapted to cold or geothermal conditions.

These characteristics are relevant to selected Martian volcanic terrains, ancient water-related geological processes, subsurface ice investigations, and astrobiological research.

However, Iceland’s dense atmosphere, abundant liquid water, active terrestrial ecosystems, and relatively mild climate differ substantially from present-day Mars.
assessments.conclusion:
Iceland receives a provisional Martian similarity score of 80.6%, classified as High.

Its strongest assessed categories are Geology and Mineralogy (88.0%), Subsurface and Natural Structures (88.0%), Atmosphere, Dust and Surface Dynamics (83.0%), and Topography and Geomorphology (80.0%).

The most valuable applications involve basaltic geology, glacial and periglacial processes, dust transport, subsurface exploration, and astrobiological instrument testing.

Iceland provides a diverse collection of terrestrial environments relevant to selected Martian exploration challenges, although the suitability of any individual field site must be assessed separately.
assessments.limitations:
Iceland does not reproduce Martian gravity, low atmospheric pressure, carbon dioxide-dominated atmosphere, global thermal conditions, or radiation environment.

Its abundant liquid water, active hydrological cycle, and extensive biological activity differ from the present Martian surface.

Icelandic glaciers and geothermal systems are useful process analogs, but they are not direct physical replicas of Martian ice deposits or ancient hydrothermal environments.

The site should therefore be used for targeted geological, operational, and astrobiological experiments rather than comprehensive environmental simulation.
assessments.methodology:
This assessment compares the terrestrial characteristics described in the supplied Icelandic research with the Martian environmental and geological reference information.

The percentages represent provisional qualitative judgments for demonstrating the website’s comparison system. They are not official NASA measurements or the output of a validated numerical scoring algorithm.

The classification scale is:

Percentage    Classificatio n

90–100%       Very high

75–less than  High 90%

50–less than  Moderate 75%

25–less than  Low 50%

0–less than 25% Very low

N/A           Not applicable

N/A values must remain distinct from zero-valued observations.

A reproducible quantitative assessment would require defined Icelandic study areas, corresponding Martian regions, comparable physical measurements, consistent spatial scales, documented normalization, and explicit weighting of variables and categories.

assessments.objective:
This assessment evaluates the suitability of the McMurdo Dry Valleys as a terrestrial analog for selected lunar polar and rocky-surface exploration activities.

The investigation focuses on frozen-ground conditions, buried ice, surface roughness, illumination, geological sampling, and robotic operations in remote polar terrain.
assessments.characterization:
The McMurdo Dry Valleys form an extensive ice-free polar desert within the Transantarctic Mountains.

The region includes broad glacial valleys, ancient moraines, rocky desert pavements, exposed sedimentary and crystalline rocks, glaciers, permanently ice-covered lakes, and exceptionally cold and dry soils.

The supplied terrestrial research describes valley-floor slopes of approximately 1–5°, steep surrounding rock walls exceeding 40°, winter temperature extremes approaching −50°C, and strong katabatic winds.

The geological assemblage includes Beacon sandstones, Ferrar dolerites, and older granitic and metamorphic rocks.

Continuous permafrost, buried ancient ice, salt accumulation, and thermal-contraction fractures are particularly relevant to polar exploration research.

However, the region retains Earth’s atmosphere, gravity, biological activity, and water-related geological processes. These differences substantially limit its direct lunar similarity.
assessments.conclusion:
The McMurdo Dry Valleys receive a provisional lunar similarity score of 45.3%, classified as Low.

The strongest assessed categories are Water, Ice and Resources (61.0%) and Topography and Geomorphology (54.0%).

The most relevant applications are buried-ice detection, frozen-ground sampling, polar navigation, and robotic exploration in cold rocky terrain.

The region’s value as a lunar analog is operational and process-specific rather than a direct match to the overall lunar environment.
assessments.limitations:
The Dry Valleys do not reproduce lunar gravity, near-vacuum conditions, space radiation, lunar regolith chemistry, or the extreme temperatures of permanently shadowed lunar regions.

Their valleys and sediments are strongly influenced by glaciation, terrestrial winds, and geological processes involving water.

The absence of representative lava tubes and impact-crater terrain also limits their suitability for certain lunar geological investigations.

The region is therefore most useful for specific polar operational and frozen-ground experiments rather than comprehensive lunar environmental simulation.
assessments.methodology:
The assessment compares the terrestrial conditions described in the supplied McMurdo Dry Valleys research with lunar geological and environmental reference information.

Scores are provisional qualitative estimates for the comparison prototype. They are not official NASA measurements or the results of a validated mathematical similarity algorithm.

Classification scale:

Percentage  Classificatio n

90–100%     Very high

75–less than  High 90%

50–less than  Moderate 75%

25–less than  Low 50%

0–less than 25% Very low

N/A           Not applicable

N/A values must remain distinct from zero-valued observations.

The overall score is a separate provisional assessment and should not be presented as a mathematically derived weighted average.

A reproducible assessment requires defined field sites, comparable physical measurements, documented normalization, spatially consistent datasets, and explicit weighting.

The Antarctic research contains broad regional descriptions and reference portals rather than a complete set of site-specific measurements. These limitations must be resolved before scientific validation.
applications: Polar ice detection: Testing instruments intended to identify buried ice beneath dry surface material.
Frozen-ground exploration: Evaluating sampling and robotic mobility in permanently frozen soils.
Polar illumination: Testing imaging and navigation under extended daylight or darkness.
Surface mobility: Investigating rover movement across rocky desert pavements and glacial blocks.
Subsurface imaging: Evaluating instruments for detecting frozen layers and fractures.
Contamination control: Testing procedures for preventing biological contamination during field sampling.

variables.label: Elevation
variables.explanation: The McMurdo Dry Valleys extend from near sea level to mountain crests exceeding 2,000 m. Lunar topography has a much larger global elevation range, measured relative to a lunar reference surface. Terrestrial and lunar elevation values cannot be compared directly without a common normalization method.
variables.utility: Testing topographic navigation and altitude-dependent field planning.

variables.label: Slope
variables.explanation: The supplied research describes relatively flat valley floors with slopes of approximately 1–5° and steep surrounding rock walls exceeding 40°. Lunar maria also contain gently sloping terrain, while crater walls and highland features can be steep.
variables.utility: Evaluating rover traction, stability, and slope-recognition systems.

variables.label: Surface roughness
variables.explanation: Antarctic desert pavements contain angular rocks, glacially transported boulders, and fractured ground. Lunar terrain also contains rocky obstacles, although lunar surface roughness depends on impact history and must be evaluated at comparable spatial scales.
variables.utility: Testing suspension systems, obstacle avoidance, and terrain-classification algorithms.

variables.label: Relief
variables.explanation: The region contains broad glacial troughs, steep mountain walls, and ancient moraine systems. The Moon has valleys, mountains, and depressions, but these are predominantly associated with impacts, volcanism, and tectonic deformation rather than glacial excavation.
variables.utility: Training robotic systems to interpret complex relief and elevation changes.

variables.label: Craters
variables.explanation: The terrestrial research identifies no prominent recent impact-crater landscape in the region. Small depressions associated with wind deflation or frozen-ground processes do not reproduce the formation mechanisms of lunar impact craters.
variables.utility: Distinguishing non-impact depressions from impact-related geological features.

variables.label: Surface obstacles
variables.explanation: Glacial erratics, angular blocks, rocky pavements, and ground fractures present obstacles comparable in operational terms to some lunar surface hazards.
variables.utility: Testing robotic obstacle detection, route selection, and autonomous navigation.

categories.utility: Rover mobility, obstacle detection, slope navigation, and terrain mapping.

variables.label: Surface temperature
variables.explanation:
The supplied research describes extremely cold annual conditions, approximately −20°C to −30°C, although these figures should not automatically be

interpreted as satellite-derived land-surface temperatures. Lunar surface temperatures vary from extremely cold polar shadows to intensely heated sunlit terrain.
variables.utility: Testing instrument operation in cold terrestrial environments.

variables.label: Maximum and minimum temperatures
variables.explanation: The terrestrial dataset reports occasional summer conditions near +5°C and winter minima approaching −50°C. Lunar permanently shadowed regions can be far colder, while illuminated lunar surfaces can become much warmer.
variables.utility: Identifying thermal equipment limitations and requirements for specialized cryogenic testing.

variables.label: Thermal variation
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys experience strong seasonal thermal changes. The Moon experiences a much longer day–night cycle and, outside some polar settings, much larger surface temperature variations.
variables.utility: Testing preliminary thermal monitoring and equipment responses to temperature changes.

variables.label: Solar illumination
variables.explanation: The research describes prolonged Antarctic summer daylight and winter darkness. These conditions offer operational comparisons with some lunar polar illumination challenges, although lunar illumination patterns depend strongly on local terrain and the Moon’s axial geometry.
variables.utility: Evaluating low-angle solar imaging, illumination-dependent navigation, and polar field planning.

variables.label: Atmospheric conditions / exosphere
variables.explanation: Antarctica retains Earth’s dense atmosphere, even under cold and dry conditions. The Moon has an extremely tenuous exosphere and essentially no atmospheric heat transfer or conventional wind.
variables.utility: Determining which tests require vacuum chambers rather than open-air terrestrial fieldwork.

categories.utility: Cold-weather equipment testing, polar illumination studies, and environmental monitoring.

variables.label: Rock type
variables.explanation: The McMurdo Dry Valleys contain Beacon sandstones, Ferrar dolerites, granitic rocks, and metamorphic basement. The Moon contains extensive anorthositic highlands, mare basalts, and impact breccias. Ferrar dolerites provide a limited mafic-rock comparison, but the overall assemblages differ.
variables.utility: Testing rock-classification instruments and identifying the limits of terrestrial lithological analogs.

variables.label: Mineralogical composition
variables.explanation: Some mafic minerals in Ferrar dolerites overlap with mineral groups found in lunar basalts. However, the region also contains quartz-rich sedimentary and granitic rocks and water-related salts that are not representative of typical lunar surface materials.
variables.utility: Evaluating mineral-identification systems and spectral discrimination.

variables.label: Chemical composition
variables.explanation: Antarctic rocks contain common silicate-forming elements, but their chemical abundances and alteration products differ from lunar mare basalts and highland anorthosites.
variables.utility: Testing geochemical classification and distinguishing different rock families.

variables.label: Surface material
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain dry sediments, angular clasts, moraines, and rocky desert pavements. Lunar regolith is produced mainly by impact fragmentation and space weathering, resulting in different grain textures and mechanical behavior.
variables.utility: Testing granular sampling, excavation, and robotic interaction with loose surface materials.

variables.label: Geological alteration
variables.explanation: Antarctic weathering includes salt crystallization, thermal contraction, and limited water-related alteration. Lunar weathering is dominated by micrometeorite impacts, solar-wind implantation, and irradiation.
variables.utility: Developing methods to distinguish terrestrial alteration from lunar space-weathering signatures.

variables.label: Geological formations
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys are dominated by glacial valleys, moraines, sedimentary sequences, and mountain structures. Lunar formations are primarily associated with impact basins, volcanic plains, and ancient tectonic structures.
variables.utility: Training geological mapping systems to distinguish different landform origins.

categories.utility: Rock identification, geological classification, and sampling-system evaluation.

variables.label: Surface water
variables.explanation: The region contains lakes and occasional meltwater processes, often beneath persistent lake ice. The exposed lunar surface does not support stable liquid water.
variables.utility: Establishing the limits of terrestrial hydrological comparisons.

variables.label: Surface ice
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain glaciers and permanently ice-covered lakes. Lunar polar surface ice occurs in much colder, frequently permanently shadowed settings and may be mixed with regolith.
variables.utility: Testing ice-recognition instruments and sampling procedures.

variables.label: Subsurface ice
variables.explanation: Ancient glacial ice can remain buried beneath dry sediment and moraine deposits. Lunar polar ice may also be concealed beneath surface material, although its origin, temperature, and physical distribution differ.
variables.utility: Evaluating ground-penetrating sensing and buried-ice detection.

variables.label: Permafrost
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain extensive frozen ground. Lunar polar regolith can remain at temperatures low enough to preserve ice for extremely long periods, but it lacks ordinary terrestrial freeze–thaw processes.
variables.utility: Testing drilling, sampling, and robotic mobility in frozen substrates.

variables.label: Hydrogen-bearing materials
variables.explanation: Hydrogen is present in Antarctic ice, lake water, and frozen sediments. Lunar hydrogen may occur in water ice, hydroxyl-bearing materials, or implanted particles. Hydrogen detection does not necessarily identify its chemical form.
variables.utility: Testing hydrogen-sensitive instruments and interpreting ice-related measurements.

variables.label: Mineral resources
variables.explanation: The region contains salts and geological materials of scientific interest. Lunar resource studies focus on oxygen-bearing minerals, metals, and polar volatiles. Antarctic materials are protected by environmental and treaty restrictions.
variables.utility: Nonextractive mineral characterization and preliminary resource-sensing studies.

categories.utility: Ice detection, frozen-ground sampling, and polar subsurface reconnaissance.

variables.label: Wind
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys experience powerful katabatic winds, with the supplied research reporting speeds of approximately 10–25 m/s. The Moon lacks a dense atmosphere capable of comparable wind.
variables.utility: Separating terrestrial atmospheric effects from lunar dust behavior.

variables.label: Abrasive dust
variables.explanation: Dry Antarctic sediments can contain fine mineral particles capable of abrading equipment. Lunar dust differs in its formation, grain morphology, electrostatic properties, and exposure history.
variables.utility: Testing seals, joints, optical surfaces, and mechanical components.

variables.label: Aeolian erosion
variables.explanation: Wind erosion shapes Antarctic ventifacts and sediments. Conventional atmospheric wind erosion does not occur on the present Moon.
variables.utility: Preventing inappropriate geological equivalence between terrestrial and lunar erosion.

variables.label: Dust storms
variables.explanation: Antarctic dust events are driven by atmospheric winds, whereas lunar dust movement involves different processes.
variables.utility: Distinguishing terrestrial dust-storm testing from lunar particle-environment simulation.

variables.label: Sediments and granular deposits
variables.explanation: Dry moraine sediments, fine mineral deposits, and rocky pavements provide granular test surfaces. Lunar regolith differs in origin, grain properties, and cohesion.
variables.utility: Evaluating excavation, granular sampling, and rover–soil interaction.

variables.label: Aerosols
variables.explanation: Antarctic marine and mineral aerosols exist within Earth’s atmosphere. There is no directly equivalent dense atmospheric aerosol system on the Moon.
variables.utility: Identifying environmental testing that cannot be transferred directly to lunar conditions.

categories.utility: Abrasion testing, particle handling, and dust-resistant equipment evaluation.

variables.label: Caves
variables.explanation: The supplied research describes very limited natural cavities, including possible salt-related openings and fractures. These differ from the volcanic cavities potentially present on the Moon.
variables.utility: Testing basic cavity detection in limited geological settings.

variables.label: Lava tubes
variables.explanation: The research identifies no lava-tube systems within the selected Dry Valleys geological environment. Lunar lava tubes are associated with ancient basaltic volcanism.
variables.utility: Identifying the need for another terrestrial analog when testing lava-tube exploration.

variables.label: Cavities and fractures
variables.explanation: Thermal-contraction cracking and fractures in frozen ground provide structural obstacles. Lunar terrain also contains fractures and collapse-related features, although their origins differ.
variables.utility: Testing fracture detection and robotic hazard recognition.

variables.label: Subsurface structure
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain sedimentary and metamorphic rock sequences overlain by frozen soils and glacial deposits. Lunar subsurface materials include impact-related regolith and volcanic or crustal layers.
variables.utility: Evaluating subsurface imaging and stratigraphic interpretation.

variables.label: Material thickness
variables.explanation: The supplied research describes variable soil and sediment thicknesses ranging from approximately one meter to several tens of meters. Lunar regolith thickness varies with terrain and geological history.
variables.utility: Testing methods for estimating the thickness of overlying material.

categories.utility: Subsurface imaging, fracture recognition, and frozen-ground reconnaissance.

variables.label: Direct biological similarity
variables.explanation: No confirmed indigenous lunar life has been identified.
variables.utility: Defining the limits of biological analog comparisons.

variables.label: Extremophile organisms
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain microbial communities adapted to extreme terrestrial environments, but these cannot be compared with confirmed lunar organisms.
variables.utility: Testing terrestrial biological instruments and contamination monitoring.

variables.label: Habitability conditions
variables.explanation: Some protected microenvironments in Antarctica support life. The exposed lunar environment lacks comparable natural biological conditions.
variables.utility: Evaluating life-support research and contamination-control procedures.

variables.label: Biosignatures
variables.explanation: Antarctic microbial traces cannot be compared with confirmed indigenous lunar biosignatures.
variables.utility: Developing methods to identify biological contamination in geological samples.

variables.label: Biological adaptations
variables.explanation: Antarctic microorganisms possess adaptations to extreme cold and desiccation, but there is no confirmed lunar biology for direct comparison.
variables.utility: Studying terrestrial microbial resilience in controlled experiments.

categories.utility: Biological instrument validation and contamination-control studies.

card.description: The McMurdo Dry Valleys provide cold, dry, rocky landscapes, frozen ground, buried ice, and prolonged seasonal darkness. These conditions offer limited comparisons with selected lunar polar exploration challenges, particularly terrain navigation and ice-related investigations.

assessments.objective:
This assessment evaluates the McMurdo Dry Valleys as a terrestrial analog for selected Martian polar, periglacial, hyperarid, and potentially habitable environments.

The investigation emphasizes subsurface ice, continuous permafrost, salt-rich soils, physical weathering, aeolian erosion, geological preservation, and microbial survival in extreme environments.
assessments.characterization:
The McMurdo Dry Valleys are among the coldest and driest ice-free regions of Antarctica.

The supplied research describes annual cold conditions of approximately −20°C to −30°C, occasional summer temperatures above freezing, and extreme winter temperatures approaching −50°C.

The region contains continuous permafrost, ancient buried glacial ice, permanently ice-covered lakes, hyperarid desert pavements, moraine deposits, salt accumulations, and extensive wind-eroded rock surfaces.

Strong katabatic winds transport fine mineral particles and shape ventifacts, while thermal contraction and salt crystallization contribute to physical weathering.

The region also supports cryptoendolithic microbial communities, which inhabit protected pore spaces within sandstone and other suitable rocks.

These features provide valuable comparisons with selected Martian periglacial landscapes, subsurface ice deposits, aeolian environments, and hypothetical ancient or protected microbial habitats.

However, the Dry Valleys retain Earth’s dense atmosphere, abundant atmospheric oxygen, terrestrial gravity, and accessible biological ecosystems. Their environmental conditions are therefore not equivalent to those of present-day Mars.
assessments.conclusion:
The McMurdo Dry Valleys receive a provisional Martian similarity score of 82.4%, classified as High.

The strongest assessed categories are Biology and Habitability (92.0%), Water, Ice and Resources (91.0%), and Atmosphere, Dust and Surface Dynamics (87.0%).

The region is particularly valuable for testing ice-detection technologies, studying permafrost and ancient ice deposits, examining aeolian erosion, and investigating microbial survival in extreme environments.

Its importance as a Martian analog lies in the similarity of selected geological and environmental processes, not in a complete reproduction of present-day Martian conditions.
assessments.limitations:
The Dry Valleys do not reproduce Martian gravity, low atmospheric pressure, carbon dioxide-dominated atmosphere, radiation exposure, or the full Martian thermal range.

Although both environments can be extremely dry and cold, Antarctica retains an active terrestrial hydrological system and biological communities.

The region also lacks representative volcanic lava tubes and extensive impact-crater fields.

Its strongest analog applications concern permafrost, buried ice, physical weathering, and astrobiology rather than complete Martian environmental simulation.

Fieldwork in Antarctica is subject to environmental protections, research permits, and applicable Antarctic Treaty requirements.

variables.label: Maximum and minimum temperatures
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys experience occasional summer temperatures above freezing and winter minima approaching −50°C. Mars experiences a broader thermal range, with very cold polar conditions and substantial daily variation.
variables.utility: Testing equipment under freezing conditions and identifying requirements for more extreme thermal simulation.

variables.label: Thermal variation
variables.explanation: Antarctic polar environments experience pronounced seasonal temperature changes associated with prolonged daylight and darkness. Mars also experiences seasonal thermal variation, although its thin atmosphere and orbital conditions produce different temperature behavior.
variables.utility: Testing long-duration environmental monitoring and thermal-response systems.

variables.label: Seasonality
variables.explanation: Antarctic seasons strongly influence daylight, temperature, frozen ground, and ice conditions. Mars also experiences significant seasons, including changes in polar carbon dioxide frost and atmospheric pressure.

variables.label: Solar illumination
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys experience prolonged summer daylight and winter darkness, with low solar angles. Martian polar regions also undergo extreme seasonal illumination changes, although the orbital and atmospheric conditions differ.
variables.utility: Testing optical navigation, low-angle imaging, and solar-energy monitoring.

variables.label: Atmospheric pressure
variables.explanation: Antarctica retains Earth’s relatively dense atmosphere, while the mean Martian surface pressure is approximately 600 Pa. Antarctic atmospheric pressure cannot reproduce the low-pressure Martian environment.
variables.utility: Identifying the need for controlled low-pressure environmental chambers.

variables.label: Rock type
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain Beacon sandstones, Ferrar dolerites, granitic rocks, and metamorphic basement. Mars contains widespread basaltic rocks as well as sedimentary formations. Ferrar dolerites and sedimentary rocks offer partial comparisons, but the overall lithologies differ.
variables.utility: Testing geological classification and rock-identification instruments.

variables.label: Mineralogical composition
variables.explanation: Antarctic rocks contain silicate minerals and soluble salts. Mars also contains silicate minerals, clay-bearing deposits, and salts, although their mineral proportions and geological histories differ.
variables.utility: Testing mineral spectroscopy and salt identification.

variables.label: Chemical composition
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys accumulate soluble salts under extremely dry conditions. Mars also contains salt-bearing materials and oxidized surface chemistry, including sulfates and oxychlorine compounds in certain regions. Direct chemical equivalence requires mineral-specific measurements.
variables.utility: Testing elemental analysis and chemical detection of salts.

variables.label: Surface material
variables.explanation: The region contains dry sediments, frozen regolith-like material, rocky pavements, and ancient moraine deposits. Mars contains loose surface materials, dust, and rock fragments, with some regions preserving ice-rich or sedimentary surfaces.
variables.utility: Evaluating sampling instruments, rover–soil interactions, and granular-material classification.

variables.label: Geological alteration
variables.explanation: Antarctic weathering is dominated by physical processes, including salt crystallization and thermal cracking, with limited liquid-water alteration in the driest environments. Some Martian terrains also preserve evidence of prolonged aridity and physical weathering.
variables.utility: Studying mineral preservation, salt-related weathering, and geological alteration signatures.

variables.label: Geological formations
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain ancient glacial valleys, moraines, ice-covered lake basins, and layered geological sequences. Mars preserves evidence of ancient water- and ice-related processes, although its landforms have different histories and scales.
variables.utility: Interpreting cold-region sedimentary structures and reconstructing geological history.

categories.utility: Geochemical analysis, salt detection, sediment characterization, and preservation studies.

variables.label: Surface water
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain lakes that remain covered by ice and may experience localized seasonal meltwater. Present-day Mars generally lacks stable exposed liquid water, but preserves evidence of past aqueous activity.
variables.utility: Investigating ice-covered water systems and understanding the limitations of present-day hydrological analogs.

variables.label: Surface ice
variables.explanation: Antarctic glaciers and permanently ice-covered lakes provide accessible environments for ice-related field research. Mars contains polar ice deposits and exposed or near-surface ice in selected regions, although their temperatures, compositions, and formation histories differ.
variables.utility: Testing ice-recognition instruments and robotic operations near frozen deposits.

variables.label: Subsurface ice
variables.explanation: Ancient glacial ice remains buried beneath dry sediments and moraine deposits in parts of the Dry Valleys. Mars also contains buried ice-rich deposits, including midlatitude and polar subsurface ice.
variables.utility: Testing ground-penetrating radar, buried-ice detection, and subsurface sampling.

variables.label: Permafrost
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain extensive continuous permafrost. Mars has widespread cold ground conditions favorable to the preservation of subsurface ice, although its temperature, pressure, and ice distribution differ.
variables.utility: Studying frozen-ground structure, sampling resistance, and ice-related geological processes.

variables.label: Hydrogen-bearing materials
variables.explanation: Antarctic ice and frozen sediments contain hydrogen-bearing water molecules. Martian neutron and gamma-ray observations can identify hydrogen enrichment associated with water ice or hydrated minerals, but do not always establish the precise chemical form.
variables.utility: Testing hydrogen-detection instruments and interpreting ice-related remote-sensing data.

variables.label: Evidence of past water
variables.explanation: Ancient moraines, glacial valleys, ice-covered lakes, and sedimentary deposits preserve evidence of long-term ice and water-related processes. Mars also preserves geological evidence of ancient rivers, lakes, glaciers, and ice-rich deposits.
variables.utility: Testing methods for reconstructing ancient hydrological and cryogenic environments.

variables.label: Mineral resources
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain salts and geological materials of scientific interest. Martian exploration considers water ice and selected mineral deposits as potential resources. Antarctic environmental protections prohibit treating the region as a resource-extraction test site without appropriate authorization.
variables.utility: Nonextractive resource identification, mineral mapping, and ice-resource reconnaissance.

categories.utility: Subsurface ice detection, frozen-ground exploration, cryogeological mapping, and reconstruction of ancient aqueous processes.

variables.label: Atmospheric pressure
variables.explanation: Antarctic atmospheric pressure is vastly greater than the mean Martian surface pressure. The cold and dry Antarctic atmosphere is not equivalent to the thin Martian atmosphere.
variables.utility: Establishing which atmospheric tests require low-pressure facilities.

variables.label: Atmospheric composition
variables.explanation: Antarctica has Earth’s nitrogen- and oxygen-rich atmosphere. Mars has a carbon dioxide-dominated atmosphere with different trace gases and aerosol conditions.
variables.utility: Defining limitations of open-air atmospheric instrument testing.

variables.label: Wind
variables.explanation: The supplied research describes katabatic winds reaching approximately 10–25 m/s. Martian winds also transport dust and sand, although the lower atmospheric density produces different forces on particles and equipment.
variables.utility: Testing wind sensors and investigating wind-driven sediment movement.

variables.label: Dust
variables.explanation: Fine mineral particles can be lifted from exposed Antarctic sediments by strong winds. Mars also contains extensive fine dust, although Martian particle chemistry and atmospheric transport differ.
variables.utility: Testing dust sensors, optical systems, and protective equipment.

variables.label: Dust storms
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys experience localized wind-driven dust events. Mars experiences dust storms at multiple spatial scales, including planet-encircling events. Their atmospheric physics and geographic extent differ.
variables.utility: Evaluating dust monitoring, sensor visibility, and equipment exposure.

variables.label: Aeolian erosion and sediments
variables.explanation: Katabatic winds shape ventifacts and redistribute fine sediments. Mars contains extensive wind-eroded rocks, dunes, and sediment deposits. Both environments demonstrate how moving particles can modify exposed geological surfaces.
variables.utility: Studying ventifact formation, sediment transport, and wind-driven erosion.

variables.label: Aerosols
variables.explanation: Antarctic air contains suspended mineral particles and marine aerosols. Mars contains mineral dust and other atmospheric aerosols, but their composition and behavior differ.
variables.utility: Testing particle-monitoring instruments and studying aerosol-related interference.

categories.utility: Dust monitoring, sediment transport, wind erosion studies, and equipment abrasion testing.

variables.label: Caves and cavities
variables.explanation: The supplied research describes limited natural cavities, including possible salt-related openings and thermal fractures. These do not reproduce the full diversity of potential Martian volcanic cavities.
variables.utility: Testing limited cavity-detection and structural imaging techniques.

variables.label: Lava tubes
variables.explanation: The selected Dry Valleys environment does not contain the lava-tube systems required for a direct Martian lava-tube comparison.
variables.utility: Identifying the need for a separate volcanic analog site.

variables.label: Fractures and faults
variables.explanation: Thermal contraction produces polygonal cracking in frozen ground, while older geological structures include fractures and faults. Mars also contains polygonal ground and tectonic fractures.
variables.utility: Testing fracture detection and identifying potential ground hazards.

variables.label: Subsurface structure
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain frozen soils, buried ice, sedimentary layers, and underlying rock sequences. Mars contains layered sedimentary and volcanic materials and ice-rich subsurface deposits.
variables.utility: Testing ground-penetrating radar and subsurface geological interpretation.

variables.label: Material thickness
variables.explanation: The supplied terrestrial research describes sediment and soil layers ranging from approximately one meter to several tens of meters. Martian subsurface deposits vary greatly in thickness and require site-specific comparison.
variables.utility: Evaluating subsurface layer-thickness estimation and stratigraphic models.

categories.utility: Subsurface imaging, ice-rich stratigraphy, fracture mapping, and robotic reconnaissance.

variables.label: Extremophile organisms
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys contain microorganisms that inhabit protected pore spaces within rocks, including cryptoendolithic microbial communities. Mars has no confirmed indigenous life, but protected subsurface microenvironments are relevant to hypotheses about potential past or present habitability.
variables.utility: Testing biological detection instruments and investigating microbial survival strategies.

variables.label: Habitability conditions
variables.explanation: The Dry Valleys combine persistent cold, severe desiccation, limited nutrients, and high ultraviolet exposure. These stresses overlap with some challenges associated with Martian environments, although Antarctic habitats remain considerably more favorable to terrestrial life.
variables.utility: Studying environmental limits for microbial survival and potential habitability indicators.

variables.label: Potential biosignatures
variables.explanation: Microbial communities can leave pigments, organic molecules, and other biological traces within rocks and frozen sediments. These provide test materials for instruments intended to identify potential biosignatures in Martian geological samples.
variables.utility: Evaluating biosignature detection and distinguishing biological from nonbiological signals.

variables.label: Biological adaptations
variables.explanation: Antarctic microorganisms may survive through slow metabolism, desiccation tolerance, and exploitation of protected rock microenvironments. These adaptations provide terrestrial models for exploring possible biological survival strategies under extreme conditions.
variables.utility: Studying microbial adaptation, preservation, and environmental tolerance.

categories.utility: Astrobiology, extremophile research, biosignature preservation, and planetary protection.

sites.terrain_classification: Polar impact crater, hyperarid Arctic desert, periglacial terrain, impact-breccia deposits, fractured carbonate bedrock, and continuous permafrost.
sites.description: Haughton Crater is a heavily eroded complex impact structure on Devon Island in the Canadian High Arctic. Its landscape contains impact-generated breccias, fractured carbonate rocks, a central structural uplift, polygonal frozen ground, seasonal snow, and localized meltwater systems. The crater provides a valuable natural laboratory for studying impact geology, polar surface operations, geological sampling, and subsurface investigations.

assessments.characterization:
Haughton is a complex impact structure situated on Devon Island in the Canadian High Arctic.

The crater formed when a high-velocity extraterrestrial object struck predominantly Paleozoic carbonate rocks, producing a large depression, impact breccias, fractured bedrock, and a central structural uplift.

Its approximate diameter is 23 km. The structure has subsequently experienced erosion and periglacial modification.

The crater has also experienced extensive terrestrial erosion and periglacial modification, making its present morphology different from that of a fresh Martian impact crater.

sites.description: The Qaidam Basin is a high-altitude, arid sedimentary basin on the northeastern Tibetan Plateau. Its landscape contains extensive dry lakebeds, salt crusts, wind-eroded sedimentary formations, dunes, and ancient lacustrine deposits. Strong evaporation, mineral precipitation, and aeolian erosion have produced distinctive geological structures, including large yardang fields and salt-rich sedimentary surfaces.
sites.scientific_relevance: Martian aeolian geomorphology, ancient lakebed interpretation, evaporite mineralogy, sedimentary stratigraphy, hypersaline environments, biosignature preservation, and robotic exploration of dry granular terrain.

assessments.objective:
This assessment examines the Qaidam Basin as a terrestrial analog for selected lunar surface exploration tasks, particularly rover navigation across flat plains, obstacle detection, granular-material handling, and remote geological classification.

It also identifies the substantial geological and environmental differences that limit Qaidam’s suitability as a lunar analog.
assessments.characterization:
The Qaidam Basin is an extensive intermontane sedimentary basin in northwestern China, characterized by high elevation, extreme aridity, ancient lake deposits, saline playas, evaporite minerals, and large wind-eroded yardang fields.

The supplied terrestrial research reports basin-floor elevations of approximately 2,600–3,200 m, central playa slopes of approximately 0°–3°, summer temperatures reaching around +30°C, and winter minima approaching −25°C to −30°C.

The basin contains halite, gypsum, other sulfates, clays, sandstones, siltstones, and fine-grained wind-transported sediments.

These features make Qaidam a strong terrestrial setting for sedimentological research, but many have no direct geological equivalent on the Moon.
assessments.conclusion:
Qaidam receives a provisional lunar similarity estimate of 30.2%, classified as Low.

Its strongest lunar category is Topography and Geomorphology (55.0%), principally because of its low-gradient plains and operationally relevant surface obstacles.

The basin should be treated as a limited operational testing environment, not a representative lunar geological or environmental analog.
assessments.limitations:
Qaidam does not reproduce lunar gravity, vacuum, radiation exposure, or extreme surface temperatures.

Its geological evolution is dominated by sedimentation, evaporation, and wind erosion rather than lunar impact gardening and volcanism.

Its salt-rich chemistry differs substantially from typical lunar regolith.

The absence of documented lava tubes and major local impact craters limits its suitability for lunar subsurface and crater exploration.
assessments.methodology:
This assessment compares the supplied Qaidam terrestrial research with the supplied lunar reference dataset.

The percentages are provisional qualitative estimates rather than measured physical similarity values.

The overall estimate is independent of the category percentages and must not be represented as a calculated weighted average.

Classification scale: Very high (90–100%); High (75–less than 90%); Moderate (50–less than 75%); Low (25–less than 50%); Very low (0–less than 25%); Not applicable (N/A).

N/A values must not be treated as zero.

A validated assessment would require site-specific sampling, normalized variables, comparable spatial scales, traceable datasets, and a documented weighting method.

variables.label: Elevation
variables.explanation: The Qaidam basin floor lies approximately 2,600–3,200 m above terrestrial sea level. Lunar elevations range across approximately 20 km relative to a lunar reference sphere. The absolute numbers are not physically comparable without using normalized local relief.
variables.utility: Testing digital elevation model processing and relative-elevation mapping.

variables.label: Slope
variables.explanation: Central saline plains have reported slopes of approximately 0°–3%, expressed in the supplied research as 0°–3°; the intended unit should be checked. In angular terms, slopes of 0°–3° overlap with the Moon’s relatively flat mare plains, often characterized by slopes of approximately 0°–5°.
variables.utility: Testing rover mobility, route selection, and slope estimation.

variables.label: Surface roughness
variables.explanation: Qaidam’s yardang ridges and salt crusts create variable roughness. Lunar terrain can also be rough, especially near impact ejecta, but lunar roughness arises from different geological processes and must be compared at consistent spatial scales.
variables.utility: Evaluating terrain-classification algorithms and wheel–surface interactions.

variables.label: Relief
variables.explanation: Qaidam is an intermontane depression bounded by major mountain ranges. Lunar basins and plains are generally impact-generated or volcanic rather than products of terrestrial-style tectonic basin evolution.
variables.utility: Training landform segmentation while testing the distinction between superficially similar relief forms.

variables.label: Impact craters
variables.explanation: The supplied research identifies no significant recent impact craters within the selected Qaidam setting. Impact cratering is a dominant lunar geological process.
variables.utility: Establishing that Qaidam is unsuitable for direct impact-crater morphology studies.

variables.label: Surface obstacles
variables.explanation: Yardang crests, salt crusts, sand dunes, and desiccated sediment blocks create navigation hazards. Lunar obstacles include angular impact blocks, regolith deposits, and collapse pits, which differ in origin and material behavior.
variables.utility: Testing obstacle detection, autonomous path planning, and rover navigation.

categories.utility: Rover route planning, terrain segmentation, and obstacle detection.

variables.label: Surface temperature
variables.explanation: Qaidam’s ground can become cold during winter and warm during summer. The supplied research does not provide a verified annual land-surface temperature series. Lunar surface temperatures vary far more strongly because of the absence of a substantial atmosphere and the long lunar day.
variables.utility: Testing surface-temperature sensors under variable terrestrial conditions.

variables.label: Maximum and minimum temperatures
variables.explanation: Qaidam’s reported summer maxima of approximately +30°C and winter minima of −25°C to −30°C are much less extreme than the Moon’s approximately +123°C maximum and −247°C minimum.
variables.utility: Determining which thermal tests require specialized chambers.

variables.label: Thermal variation
variables.explanation: The basin experiences pronounced daily and seasonal thermal changes. Lunar surface thermal cycles can reach approximately 280–300 K in amplitude at some low-latitude locations, far exceeding ordinary terrestrial variation.
variables.utility: Testing temperature logging and preliminary thermal-cycling procedures.

variables.label: Solar illumination
variables.explanation: Qaidam receives strong solar radiation under generally clear skies. Lunar illumination occurs without substantial atmospheric scattering, and its day–night cycle lasts approximately 29.5 Earth days.
variables.utility: Testing solar exposure monitoring and optical imaging under bright conditions.

variables.label: Atmospheric conditions / exosphere
variables.explanation: Qaidam has a terrestrial atmosphere, although its elevation reduces ambient pressure. The Moon has an extremely tenuous exosphere and no comparable atmospheric pressure.
variables.utility: Identifying the need for vacuum-chamber qualification.

categories.utility: Environmental sensor testing and preliminary thermal monitoring.

variables.label: Rock type
variables.explanation: Qaidam contains lacustrine sediments, sandstones, siltstones, and evaporites. Lunar bedrock is dominated by igneous and impact-related lithologies.
variables.utility: Testing lithological classification and detecting nonanalog rock types.

variables.label: Mineralogical composition
variables.explanation: Qaidam contains quartz, feldspars, clay minerals, halite, gypsum, and other evaporites. Lunar materials are dominated by plagioclase, pyroxene, olivine, and impact glass.
variables.utility: Evaluating spectral mineral identification and classification errors.

variables.label: Chemical composition
variables.explanation: Qaidam’s salt-rich deposits contain abundant sodium, chlorine, magnesium, and sulfate-bearing phases. Lunar regolith chemistry is dominated by silicate and oxide minerals with different relative abundances.
variables.utility: Testing geochemical instruments and identifying chemically dissimilar materials.

variables.label: Surface material
variables.explanation: Qaidam’s loose silts, sands, and granular deposits may offer partial mechanical analogs for regolith handling. Lunar regolith differs in grain shape, cohesion, impact-glass content, and electrostatic behavior.
variables.utility: Preliminary excavation and granular-sampling tests.

variables.label: Geological alteration
variables.explanation: Qaidam is strongly modified by wind abrasion, evaporation, and salt precipitation. Lunar space weathering is dominated by micrometeorite bombardment, solar-wind implantation, and radiation.
variables.utility: Distinguishing terrestrial weathering products from lunar space-weathering signatures.

variables.label: Geological formations
variables.explanation: Yardangs, lacustrine deposits, playas, and alluvial fans have no close process-level counterparts in the modern lunar landscape.
variables.utility: Testing geological feature recognition and rejecting inappropriate lunar analog classifications.

categories.utility: Testing mineral identification and differentiating terrestrial sedimentary signals from lunar geological signatures.

variables.label: Surface water
variables.explanation: Qaidam contains residual saline lakes and intermittent watercourses. Stable exposed liquid water is absent from the lunar surface.
variables.utility: Identifying terrestrial hydrological processes that cannot be transferred to lunar models.

variables.label: Surface ice
variables.explanation: The central basin is not characterized by persistent surface ice. Lunar polar ice can occur in permanently shadowed cold traps.
variables.utility: Excluding the central basin from primary lunar surface-ice analog testing.

variables.label: Subsurface ice
variables.explanation: The supplied research does not document subsurface ice in the central desert plains. This absence of evidence does not establish a measured ice concentration of zero.
variables.utility: Prioritizing field verification before attempting ice-related comparisons.

variables.label: Permafrost
variables.explanation: Discontinuous mountain permafrost occurs around the basin, but it should not be assigned to the central playa terrain without local evidence. Lunar polar regolith can remain permanently cold under fundamentally different conditions.
variables.utility: Separating basin-floor and surrounding mountain environments in resource assessments.

variables.label: Hydrogen-bearing materials
variables.explanation: Hydrated clays and subsurface brines contain hydrogen-bearing compounds. Lunar hydrogen may occur in water ice, hydroxyl-bearing materials, or solar-wind-implanted hydrogen.
variables.utility: Testing hydrogen-sensitive instruments while distinguishing different hydrogen reservoirs.

variables.label: Mineral resources
variables.explanation: Qaidam contains economically significant salt and evaporite deposits. Lunar resource priorities include oxygen-bearing silicates, metals, and polar volatiles rather than terrestrial-style evaporite deposits.
variables.utility: Testing resource mapping workflows and mineral identification.

categories.utility: Hydrated-mineral sensing and identification of analog limitations.

variables.label: Wind
variables.explanation: Qaidam experiences strong regional winds, while the Moon has no dense atmosphere capable of generating aerodynamic winds.
variables.utility: Establishing limits for lunar environmental simulation.

variables.label: Abrasive dust
variables.explanation: Fine Qaidam sediments can be abrasive, but lunar dust is produced primarily through impacts and can have distinctive angular, glass-rich, and electrostatic properties.
variables.utility: Preliminary dust-ingress and mechanical abrasion tests.

variables.label: Dust storms
variables.explanation: Atmospheric dust storms have no direct lunar equivalent. Lunar particle transport is associated with impacts, spacecraft disturbances, and potentially electrostatic processes.
variables.utility: Preventing physically invalid comparisons.

variables.label: Aeolian erosion
variables.explanation: Qaidam’s yardangs are sculpted by wind abrasion and deflation. Lunar terrain is not shaped by atmospheric wind erosion.
variables.utility: Differentiating aeolian morphology from impact-generated lunar landforms.

variables.label: Sediments and granular deposits
variables.explanation: Qaidam contains loess-like silts, sands, and lacustrine clays. Lunar granular deposits consist largely of impact-generated regolith and volcanic material.
variables.utility: Evaluating granular sampling systems while accounting for different sediment origins.

variables.label: Aerosols
variables.explanation: Qaidam’s mineral aerosols require an atmosphere. The Moon does not have an equivalent atmospheric aerosol system.
variables.utility: Defining instrument-testing limitations.

categories.utility: Mechanical dust testing and differentiation of terrestrial and lunar sediment processes.

variables.label: Caves
variables.explanation: The supplied research does not identify significant caves in the selected sedimentary basin environment. Lunar collapse pits and possible subsurface cavities are associated with different geological processes.
variables.utility: Excluding Qaidam from primary lunar cave analog selection.

variables.label: Lava tubes
variables.explanation: No lava tubes are documented in the selected Qaidam sedimentary terrain. Lunar lava tubes originate through ancient volcanic activity.
variables.utility: Identifying the need for volcanic analog locations.

variables.label: Cavities and fractures
variables.explanation: Qaidam contains desiccation cracks and salt-related contraction fractures. Lunar fractures can form through impacts, tectonic stresses, and volcanic processes.
variables.utility: Testing fracture-detection algorithms and shallow subsurface imaging.

variables.label: Subsurface structure
variables.explanation: Qaidam’s subsurface contains alternating lacustrine, evaporitic, and alluvial layers. Lunar subsurface layers commonly reflect impact deposition and volcanic activity.
variables.utility: Testing stratigraphic interpretation while distinguishing different depositional processes.

variables.label: Material thickness
variables.explanation: Qaidam contains sedimentary basin fill reaching kilometer-scale thicknesses. Lunar regolith and impact deposits have different thickness distributions and formation histories.
variables.utility: Testing radar-based layer-thickness estimation.

categories.utility: Shallow fracture mapping and radar-based layer detection.

variables.label: Extremophile organisms
variables.explanation: Qaidam contains terrestrial microorganisms, but there are no confirmed lunar organisms.
variables.utility: Testing biological contamination detection.

variables.label: Habitability conditions
variables.explanation: Qaidam’s terrestrial microbial habitats do not establish equivalent lunar habitats.
variables.utility: Supporting controlled biological instrument tests.

variables.label: Biosignatures
variables.explanation: Terrestrial biosignatures have no confirmed indigenous lunar counterpart.
variables.utility: Differentiating biological contamination from nonbiological signals.

variables.label: Biological adaptations
variables.explanation: Terrestrial microbial adaptations cannot be directly compared with unknown lunar biological systems.
variables.utility: Evaluating terrestrial biological responses without implying lunar life.
